{{Short description|Theorem of matrix algebra of invariance properties under basis transformations}}
'''Sylvester's law of inertia''' is a [[theorem]] in [[matrix algebra]] about certain properties of the [[Gram matrix|coefficient matrix]] of a [[real number|real]] [[quadratic form]] that remain [[invariant (mathematics)|invariant]] under a [[change of basis]]. Namely, if <math>S</math> is a [[symmetric matrix]], then for any [[invertible matrix]] <math>P</math>, the numbers of positive, negative, and zero [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalues]] of <math>S' = PSP^\mathsf{T}</math> are constant (i.e., the inertia of <math>S'</math> is constant). This result is particularly useful when <math>S'</math> is diagonal, as the inertia of a [[diagonal matrix]] can easily be obtained by looking at the signs of its diagonal elements.

This property is named after [[James Joseph Sylvester]], who published its proof in 1852.<ref name=syl852>{{cite journal | last=Sylvester | first=James Joseph | authorlink=James Joseph Sylvester | title=A demonstration of the theorem that every homogeneous quadratic polynomial is reducible by real orthogonal substitutions to the form of a sum of positive and negative squares | journal=Philosophical Magazine | series=4th Series | volume=4 | issue=23 | pages=138–142 | year=1852 | url=http://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~aar/sylv/inertia.pdf | doi=10.1080/14786445208647087 | accessdate=2008-06-27}}
</ref><ref name=norm>{{cite book | last=Norman | first= C. W. | title=Undergraduate algebra | publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] | pages=360–361 | year=1986 | isbn=978-0-19-853248-4}}
</ref>

== Statement <span class="anchor" id="Statement of the theorem"></span> ==
Let <math>S</math> be a symmetric square matrix of order <math>n</math> with [[real number|real]] entries. Any [[non-singular matrix|non-singular]] square matrix <math>P</math> of the same order is said to transform <math>S</math> into another symmetric matrix {{tmath| S' {{=}} PSP^\mathsf{T} }}, also of order {{tmath| n }}, where <math>P^\mathsf{T}</math> is the transpose of {{tmath| P }}. It is also said that matrices <math>S</math> and <math>S'</math> are [[Matrix congruence|congruent]]. If <math>S</math> is the coefficient matrix of some quadratic form on {{tmath| \R^n }}, then <math>S'</math> is the coefficient matrix of the same form after the change of basis defined by {{tmath| P }}.

A symmetric matrix <math>S</math> can always be transformed in this way into a [[diagonal matrix]] <math>D</math> which has entries only {{tmath| 0 }}, {{tmath| +1 }}, {{tmath| -1 }} along the diagonal. Sylvester's law of inertia states that the number of diagonal entries of each kind is an invariant of {{tmath| S }}, i.e., does not depend on the matrix <math>P</math> used.

The number of {{tmath| +1 }}'s, denoted {{tmath| n_+ }}, is called the '''positive index of inertia''' of {{tmath| S }}, and the number of {{tmath| -1 }}'s, denoted {{tmath| n_- }}, is called the '''negative index of inertia''' of {{tmath|S}}. The number of {{tmath| 0 }}'s, denoted {{tmath| n_0 }}, is the dimension of the [[kernel (linear algebra)|null space]] of {{tmath| S }}, known as the '''nullity''' of {{tmath| S }}. These numbers satisfy the obvious relation
: {{tmath|n_{0}+n_{+}+n_{-} {{=}} n}}.

The difference <math> \mathrm{sgn}(S) = n_+ - n_- </math> is usually called the '''signature''' of {{tmath| S }}. However, some authors use that term for the triple <math>(n_0,n_+,n_-)</math> consisting of the nullity, the positive, and the negative indices of inertia of {{tmath| S }}. For a non-degenerate form of a given dimension, these are equivalent data; but in general, the triple yields more data.

If the matrix <math>S</math> has the property that every principal upper left <math>k \times k</math> [[minor (determinant)|minor]] <math>\Delta_k</math> is non-zero, then the negative index of inertia is equal to the number of sign changes in the sequence
: {{tmath|1= \Delta_0 = 1, \Delta_1, \ldots, \Delta_n = \det S }}.

== Statement in terms of eigenvalues ==
The law can also be stated as follows: two symmetric square matrices <math>S</math> and <math>S'</math> of the same size have the same numbers of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues if and only if they are [[Matrix congruence|congruent]]<ref>{{cite book | last=Carrell | first=James B. | title=Groups, Matrices, and Vector Spaces: A Group Theoretic Approach to Linear Algebra | date=2017 | publisher=Springer | isbn=978-0-387-79428-0 | page=313}}</ref> (i.e., {{tmath| S' {{=}} PSP^\mathsf{T} }} for some non-singular square matrix {{tmath| P }}).

The positive and negative indices of a symmetric matrix <math>S</math> are also the numbers of positive and negative [[eigenvalue]]s of {{tmath| S }}. Any symmetric real matrix <math>S</math> has an [[eigendecomposition]] of the form {{tmath| QEQ^\mathsf{T} }}, where <math>E</math> is a diagonal matrix containing the eigenvalues of {{tmath| S }}, and <math>Q</math> is an [[Orthogonal matrix|orthogonal]] square matrix containing the eigenvectors. The matrix <math>E</math> can be written {{tmath| E {{=}} WDW^\mathsf{T} }}, where <math>D</math> is diagonal with entries {{tmath| 0,+1,-1 }}, and <math>W</math> is diagonal with each {{tmath| W_{i,i} {{=}} \sqrt{ \vert E_{i,i} \vert } }}. The matrix <math>P = QW</math> transforms <math>D</math> to {{tmath| S }}, since {{tmath|1= S = QEQ^\mathsf{T} = QW ~ D ~ W^\mathsf{T} \! Q^\mathsf{T} }}.

== Statement in terms of quadratic forms ==
A real [[quadratic form]] <math>q</math> in <math>n</math> variables (or on an {{tmath|n}}-dimensional real vector space) can, by a suitable change of basis (by non-singular linear transformation from <math>x</math> to {{tmath| y }}), be brought to the diagonal form
: {{tmath|1= q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i {x_i}^2 }}, with each {{tmath| a_i \in \{ 0,1,-1 \} }}.

Sylvester's law of inertia states that the number of coefficients of a given sign is an invariant of {{tmath| q }}, i.e., does not depend on a particular choice of diagonalizing basis.

Expressed geometrically, the law of inertia says that all maximal subspaces on which the restriction of the quadratic form is [[definite bilinear form|positive definite]] (respectively, negative definite) have the same [[dimension (linear algebra)|dimension]]. These dimensions are the positive and negative indices of inertia of {{tmath|q}}.

== Generalizations ==
Two [[complex matrices]] (i.e., with [[Complex number|complex]] entries) <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are said to be {{tmath| \mathbf{*} }}'''-congruent''' if (and only if) there exists a non-singular complex matrix <math>P</math> such that {{tmath| B {{=}} PAP^* }}, where <math>P^*</math> denotes the [[conjugate transpose]] of {{tmath|P}}.

The definition of inertia is still valid for a [[Hermitian matrix]], as its eigenvalues are always real numbers.

Sylvester's law of inertia can be generalized to complex matrices:<br>Two Hermitian matrices <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are {{tmath|*}}-congruent if and only if they have the same inertia.

[[Alexander Ostrowski|Ostrowski]] proved a quantitative generalization of Sylvester's law of inertia:<ref>{{Cite journal | last=Ostrowski | first=Alexander M. | date=1959 | title=A quantitative formulation of Sylvester's law of inertia | url=https://www.pnas.org/content/pnas/45/5/740.full.pdf | journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | volume=A quantitative formulation of Sylvester's law of inertia | issue=5 | pages=740–744 | doi=10.1073/pnas.45.5.740 | pmid=16590437 | pmc=222627 | bibcode=1959PNAS...45..740O | doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1=Higham | first1=Nicholas J. | last2=Cheng | first2=Sheung Hun | date=1998 | title=Modifying the inertia of matrices arising in optimization | journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications | language=en | volume=275-276 | pages=261–279 | doi=10.1016/S0024-3795(97)10015-5 | doi-access=free}}</ref><br>If two complex matrices <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are {{tmath|*}}-congruent, with {{tmath| B {{=}} PAP^*}} where <math>P</math> is a non-singular complex matrix, then their eigenvalues <math>\lambda_j</math> are related by
: {{tmath|\lambda_{j}(B) {{=}} \theta_j ~ \lambda_{j}(A)}},
where {{tmath|j {{=}} 1, \ldots, n}}, and each <math>\theta_j</math> is such that
: {{tmath|\lambda_{n}(PP^*) \leq \theta_j \leq \lambda_{1}(PP^*)}}.<br><br>

A theorem due to Ikramov generalizes the law of inertia to [[normal matrices]]:<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Ikramov | first1=Kh. D. | title=On the inertia law for normal matrices | journal=Doklady Mathematics | date=2001 | volume=64 | pages=141–142}}</ref><br>Two normal matrices <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are {{tmath|*}}-congruent if and only if they have the same number of eigenvalues on each [[Open set|open]] ray from the origin in the [[complex plane]].{{efn|For example, the matrices <math display="block">A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & i \end{bmatrix}
\quad \text{and} \quad
B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4i \end{bmatrix}</math> are both normal.<br>
{{tmath|A}} and {{tmath|B}} are {{tmath|*}}-congruent: <math display="block">B = M^* \! A ~\! M, \quad \text{where} \quad
M^* = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad
M = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}.</math><br>
Both {{tmath|A}} and {{tmath|B}} have two eigenvalues on the open ray {{tmath|\mathbf{]} 0, 1 )}} and one eigenvalue on the open ray {{tmath|\mathbf{]} 0, i )}}; denoting by respectively {{tmath|\lambda_j}} and {{tmath|\mu_j}} the eigenvalues of {{tmath|A}} and {{tmath|B}}: <math display="block">\begin{matrix}
\lambda_1 &= & 1, & \quad & \lambda_2 &= & 3, & \quad & \lambda_3 &= & i; \\
\mu_1 &= & 4 - \sqrt{13}, & \quad & \mu_2 &= & 4 + \sqrt{13}, & \quad & \mu_3 &= & 4i.
\end{matrix}</math>}}
